cases.title: `api_request` declares the fields its executor returns.
`embed_search` declares the fields its executor returns.
`llm_router` declares the fields its executor returns.
`notify` declares the fields its executor returns.
`webhook_out` declares the fields its executor returns.
`for_each` declares the fields its executor returns.
`log` declares the fields its executor returns.
A pass-through kind declares NO field shape — null, never an empty list.
cases.note: null means nobody declared. Reading it as [] refuses every valid reference on the kind.

cases.title: `merge` in concat mode declares neither a shape nor a relation.
cases.note: It emits a LIST, whose elements are not addressable as top-level fields. [] would claim 'emits no fields', which is false and would refuse every reference.

skip.rust: fancy-flow-rs cannot resolve a config-dependent relation in-process: NodeKind derives Clone + PartialEq, so it carries EmitsRelation::Dynamic as a MARKER rather than a closure. It answers "dynamic" here -- which is honest and is NOT null: null claims nobody declared, about a kind that has. Requiring null would force it either to fail forever or to lie. Every other row in this table runs on Rust; this is the one question it cannot be asked.

cases.title: `llm_call` is config-dependent, and says so rather than staying silent.
cases.note: A consumer must tell 'declared, unresolvable here' from 'nobody declared': the first means ask the host, the second means fall back to your own knowledge. Collapsing them makes a fixed table answer a config-dependent question.

cases.title: `user_input` emits the keys its author defined, so it is dynamic too.
`switch_case` declares the relation `input`.
`output` declares the relation `input`.
`human_approval` declares the relation `input`.
`manual_trigger` declares the relation `input`.
cases.note: `input-map-merged`, not `input` or `inputs-merged`. This kind merges the raw input MAP, whose shape depends on POSITION: collectInputs seeds an entry node flat and keys every other node by handle, so the same kind with an inbound edge emits {cron, timezone, in: {...}}. `merge` unions each port's PAYLOAD, which is a different operation -- two names rather than one name plus a positional rule a reader has to know.

cases.title: `variable` declares the relation `expression:value`.
An expression relation carries the config key it reads — `value`, not `expression`.
cases.note: A consumer hardcoding 'the field called expression' has copied the runtime's knowledge one level down, which is what carrying the key removes. `transform` reads `expression`; `variable` reads `value`.

cases.title: `wait` NESTS its input under a key, so it declares fields and NO relation.
cases.note: A relation with no destination can only express a TOP-LEVEL merge. emits:'input' here would make a reader accept {{ in.<any inbound field> }} at top level, which resolves to nothing at run time. This row is why merge-or-nest must be read off the executor before a relation is assigned.

cases.title: `schedule_trigger` declares BOTH, because its merge is genuinely top-level.
cases.note: `input-map-merged`, not `input` or `inputs-merged`. This kind merges the raw input MAP, whose shape depends on POSITION: collectInputs seeds an entry node flat and keys every other node by handle, so the same kind with an inbound edge emits {cron, timezone, in: {...}}. `merge` unions each port's PAYLOAD, which is a different operation -- two names rather than one name plus a positional rule a reader has to know.

cases.title: `webhook_trigger` declares no relation — its choice is DATA-dependent.
cases.note: `inputs.payload ?? inputs` cannot be answered from config, so no relation is honest. Under-claiming is free.
